concept: Atlas Stream Processing partition idleness versus window idleness
summary: Source-anchored research for Atlas Stream Processing partition idleness versus window idleness. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: For $tumblingWindow and $hoppingWindow, idleTimeout controls closing windows when $source is idle. It belongs to the window stage; partitionIdleTimeout belongs to $source and governs individual Kafka partitions. (high confidence)

Both tumbling and hopping references prohibit idleTimeout and allowedLateness when boundary is processingTime. Their documented boundary default is eventTime. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Independent conceptual context: Apache Flink and Confluent describe downstream watermarks as constrained by the slowest parallel input; Apache documents idleness detection to prevent inactive inputs from stalling progress. These sources explain the general mechanism, not Atlas timer implementation. (medium confidence)

With a Kafka source, an idle partition can prevent watermark progress and leave a window without output. The architecture reference identifies partitionIdleTimeout as the mitigation; MongoDB diagnostic guidance also lists this condition for a STARTED processor with zero windowed output. (high confidence)

The $source reference documents partitionIdleTimeout as disabled by default. Its duration uses size and unit, supporting ms, second, minute, hour, or day. This default was verified in the 2026-10-14 documentation snapshot. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Both window-stage references say the idle timer starts as soon as $source becomes idle, and describe closing after the greater of the remaining window time and idleTimeout. Their example closes a 12:00–13:00 window last active at 12:02 at 14:02 for a two-hour timeout, or at 13:00 for a ten-minute timeout. Treat this as reference behavior pending resolution of the architecture-page discrepancy. (medium confidence)

A published MongoDB pipeline example combines a five-second partitionIdleTimeout on Kafka $source with a ten-second idleTimeout on a thirty-second tumbling window. These durations are settings in that example, not universal recommendations. (medium confidence)

Forced window progress has a lateness consequence: events arriving after their window closes are late, and Atlas can route them to a configured dead letter queue. Choosing an idleness timeout therefore needs to account for expected event delays. (medium confidence)

Diagnostic inference: distinguish one silent Kafka partition while other partitions produce data from source-wide silence. Inspect partitionIdleTimeout for the former and window idleTimeout for the latter; the settings address different progress conditions. (medium confidence)
